title: Brand Authorization in Russia: A Guide for Turkish Brands
excerpt: Brand Authorization Process, Distribution Agreements and Marketplace Requirements for Turkish brands entering the Russian market.

blocks.text: For Turkish brands entering the Russian market, shipping products to Russia and listing them on a marketplace is only one part of the market entry process.
It is equally important to determine who will represent the brand in Russia, who will be authorized to sell its products, and under what conditions the brand can be used.

This becomes particularly important when selling through marketplaces such as Wildberries and Ozon, where sellers may be required to provide documents proving their relationship with the brand and the authenticity of the products. Brand authorization agreements, distribution agreements and, where necessary, licensing agreements should be considered from the beginning of the market entry process.
What Is Brand Authorization?
Brand authorization is the process through which a brand owner grants a company or business partner in Russia specific rights to represent, sell or use the brand within defined commercial conditions.

blocks.title: Important Distinction
blocks.text: Representing a brand and granting the right to use a trademark are not necessarily the same thing.

blocks.text: The exact scope of these rights should be clearly defined in the agreement.
Why Is Brand Authorization Important When Entering Russia?

An incomplete or unclear documentation structure can create problems during the Russian sales operation, particularly on marketplaces. For example, a seller may state: "We purchase these products directly from the manufacturer in Turkey." But from a marketplace perspective, another question may be more important: "How can you prove that you are authorized to sell and use this brand?"

Wildberries distinguishes between different statuses such as brand owner, licensee, distributor, dealer and reseller, and may request documents proving the seller's relationship with the brand and the authenticity of the products.
Brand authorization should not be treated as a document to prepare after entering the Russian market. It should be considered as part of the market entry strategy from the beginning.
Is Brand Authorization the Same as a Distribution Agreement?
No. Although these concepts are often used together, they can serve different commercial and legal purposes.
Brand Authorization

Brand authorization gives a company specific rights to represent or use a brand for defined purposes. For example: "Company X is an authorized representative of our brand in the Russian Federation." The agreement may define exactly what this authorization covers.
Distribution Agreement

A distributor may take responsibility for a broader commercial operation, including purchasing, importing, distributing and selling products, managing sales channels, maintaining inventory, and meeting sales targets. A distribution relationship may therefore involve product supply, sales, distribution and commercial targets together. However, even where a distributor is appointed, the rights to use the brand should be clearly addressed in the contractual structure.
Brand Authorization Models for the Russian Market
There is no single model that works for every brand. The appropriate structure depends on the Turkish manufacturer's business model and Russian market strategy.
1. Authorized Reseller Model

A Russian company purchases the products from the brand and sells them through agreed channels: Turkish Brand → Authorized Russian Reseller → Wildberries / Ozon. This model can be particularly practical when starting marketplace sales.

3. Exclusive Distribution

A brand owner may appoint one partner as its exclusive distributor in Russia. However, this decision requires careful consideration — exclusivity can effectively mean that only this partner is authorized to sell the brand within the agreed territory or channel.
Exclusivity should ideally be defined together with territory, duration, sales channels and performance targets — this allows the brand owner to maintain greater control over the relationship.
4. Non-Exclusive Authorization

The brand owner may work with several sellers or distributors in the same market, for example a Wildberries partner, an Ozon partner, a B2B distributor and authorized dealers. This model can provide greater flexibility, particularly for brands entering Russia for the first time and testing the market.
What Should a Brand Authorization Agreement Include?
A strong authorization agreement should not simply state "this company is authorized to sell our products in Russia." The scope of the authorization should be clearly defined.
The trademark's legal status in Russia should also be reviewed separately.

blocks.title: 3. Scope of Authorization — one of the most important sections
items: Use the brand in promotional materials?

blocks.text: 4. Territory: the authorization can cover the entire Russian Federation, or specific territories and/or sales channels. The geographical scope should be clearly stated in the agreement.
For example, one partner may be authorized specifically for Wildberries while another manages Ozon.

6. Agreement Duration: authorization does not necessarily need to be indefinite — the agreement may specify 12 months, 24 months, or another defined period. Renewal conditions should also be clearly established.
7. Exclusivity: if the partner is appointed as an exclusive distributor, exclusivity should be explicitly defined (e.g. "exclusive distributor of the brand in the Russian Federation").

It can also be useful to include performance conditions such as a minimum annual sales target — this helps protect the brand owner from granting exclusivity without receiving sufficient commercial performance in return.
8. Marketplace Authorization

Wildberries may require documentation demonstrating the seller's relationship with a brand, depending on whether the seller is a brand owner, licensee, distributor, dealer or another type of authorized seller. For licensees and representatives, documents such as licensing agreements or powers of attorney may be relevant.

The agreement should explicitly address whether the authorized party may use the brand on marketplaces such as Wildberries and Ozon — this can significantly simplify the operational process when marketplace documentation is requested.
The brand owner may also establish an approval process for advertising materials and visual assets.

11. Sub-Distribution and Transfer of Rights: if the authorized distributor should not be allowed to transfer its rights to another company, this should be explicitly stated (e.g. appointment of a sub-distributor requires the prior written approval of the brand owner). This helps the brand owner maintain control over how its rights are used in the Russian market.
Should Turkish Brands Register Their Trademark in Russia?
A trademark registered in Turkey does not automatically provide the same level of protection in Russia. Trademark protection in Russia should therefore be assessed separately.

For Turkish brands planning a long-term presence in Russia, the following sequence should be considered: Trademark research → Trademark protection → Authorization → Marketplace. This becomes particularly important before investing heavily in marketing, marketplace operations and distribution.
Why Is Brand Authorization Important on Wildberries?
Wildberries may request documentation proving the seller's relationship with a brand and the authenticity of products.

This means that simply saying "we purchased these products from the manufacturer in Turkey" may not always be enough to demonstrate the full scope of the seller's authorization to use the brand. There is an important difference between proving that a product is authentic and proving that the seller has the right to use and represent the brand.

A consignment agreement and a brand authorization agreement should not automatically be considered the same document — each serves a different purpose.
Common Mistakes Turkish Brands Make

items: "We have a distribution agreement, so no separate brand authorization is necessary." — Not every distribution agreement automatically provides the same scope of trademark usage rights.
"Our Turkish trademark registration is enough." — Trademark protection in Russia should be assessed separately.
"Marketplaces do not ask for brand documents." — Marketplaces may request documentation proving brand rights and product authenticity.
"Let's give the partner exclusivity and discuss sales targets later." — If exclusivity is granted, performance conditions should ideally be defined at the same time.

"We appointed a distributor, so they control everything in Russia." — The brand owner should determine from the beginning how much control it wants over pricing, marketing, marketplace operations, brand communication and customer experience.

Conclusion: Brand Authorization Is Part of the Russia Market Entry Strategy

Shipping products to Russia and listing them on a marketplace does not, by itself, mean that a brand has established a proper market presence. The brand should clearly define who represents it, where it can be sold, which channels can be used, who can use the brand, and how much control remains with the brand owner.

For brands selling through Wildberries and other marketplaces, proper documentation of brand rights and product authenticity can become an important operational requirement. Brand authorization should not be treated as a simple legal formality — it should be considered part of the overall Russia market entry strategy.
